bill.title: the Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act of 2025
bill.description: The bill would change Title IX, the federal law against sex discrimination in schools and colleges that receive federal money. Those schools could not let a person the bill classifies as male take part in a sports program for women or girls. The bill would decide sex “based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” The bill would still allow males to train or practice with those teams if no female loses a team place, a chance to play, a scholarship, admission to a school or another sports benefit. The bill also orders a federal study of benefits that girls could lose.

claims.title: The sports rule and its definition of sex
claims.statement: This rule covers a school or college that receives federal money and runs, sponsors or facilitates sports. It may not let a person whose sex is male, as the bill defines it, take part in a sports program designated for women or girls. The bill defines sex for this rule based only on reproductive biology and genetics at birth.
claims.classification_reason: Direct statutory text, checked word for word against the bill as passed by the House. It is background, not a vote. Accepting it does not accept any argument that uses it.
claims.section: H.R.28 (Engrossed in House), Sec. 2, adding 20 U.S.C. 1681(d)(1)–(2)
claims.source_quote: It shall be a violation of subsection (a) for a recipient of Federal financial assistance who operates, sponsors, or facilitates athletic programs or activities to permit a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls. “(2) For the purposes of this subsection, sex shall be recognized based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.
claims.scope_html: The rule covers only programs designated for women or girls at places that receive federal money. The definition applies “For the purposes of this subsection” [1]. The text does not name transgender, nonbinary or intersex students, and it does not set a way to check sex.
claims.background_html: A recipient of federal financial assistance is an organization that receives federal money. Title IX is the federal law against sex discrimination in education. It “prohibits sex discrimination in federally funded education programs.” [2]
claims.support_html: The bill says it “shall be a violation of subsection (a) for a recipient of Federal financial assistance” [1] to allow this participation. It adds that “sex shall be recognized based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1]

claims.title: The law in force on January 14, 2025
claims.statement: On January 14, 2025, federal law had no express rule on transgender athletes. Some schools, states and sports organizations let transgender girls and women compete in girls’ and women’s sports, with or without conditions. Others did not.
claims.classification_reason: Adequately sourced by Congress’s research office and the sports rules themselves, and no response challenges it. It sets the comparison; it is not a vote and does not show that any change is good or bad.
claims.scope_html: Practice differed by place. The bill would change the rule only where this participation was allowed. Later events, such as the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) rule change on February 6, 2025, are not part of this comparison.
claims.background_html: The Congressional Research Service (CRS) is Congress’s research office. The report quoted here was updated in August 2025. Regulations are rules written by a government agency. The NCAA is the main college sports organization.
claims.support_html:
CRS says: “Neither the statute nor the regulations currently address how Title IX applies to transgender athletes.” [1] The 2024 Title IX regulations were already canceled, because “a federal district court vacated them in January 2025.” [1] Older rules allowed separate teams: “Long-standing Title IX regulations permit separation of the sexes in school sports programs provided schools offer equal athletic opportunities.” [2]

CRS also says some places let transgender students compete “with no particular requirements or restrictions.” [3] College sports used limits on testosterone, a hormone: “Between January 19, 2022, and February 6, 2025, the NCAA called for the participation of transgender athletes to be regulated on a sport-by-sport basis.” [4] Elsewhere, states had laws “requiring student-athletes to participate on teams according to their sex assigned at birth.” [3]

claims.title: Physical mismatch in women’s contact sports
claims.statement: In women’s contact competition, such as rugby, athletes who went through male puberty can keep differences in size, speed and force after lowering testosterone. These differences can raise the risk of collision injury for smaller players.
claims.classification_reason: This modest collision-risk proposition has no retained response disputing it. Modeling limits, international scope and low-certainty fitness evidence remain visible qualifications; they do not require an extra shared vote about a possibility.
claims.scope_html: This claim covers contact competition only. It does not cover athletes who did not go through male puberty. The evidence is not a measured count of injuries involving transgender players. World Rugby’s conclusion was for “the international level of the game” [1], and its guidance does “not preclude national unions from flexibility in their application of the guidelines at the domestic/community level of the game” [1]. Rejecting this claim does not reject other routes in an argument.
claims.background_html: World Rugby is the international body for rugby, a sport with frequent physical contact. Testosterone is a hormone. A tackle is when one player stops another by force.
claims.support_html:
World Rugby says: “Forces and inertia faced by a smaller and slower player during frequent collisions are significantly greater when in contact with a much larger, faster player.” [2] It adds that “large discrepancies create greater risks for smaller and slower players” [3]. It concludes that “this comparatively small effect of testosterone reduction allows substantial and meaningful differences to remain.” [2]

The limits are also in the sources. World Rugby’s summary says: “To date, no direct studies on trans women rugby players.” [4] A 2026 review reports “higher lean mass” [5] in transgender women but says “their physical fitness was comparable.” [5] It calls the evidence “mostly low certainty” [5].

prerequisite_paths.reason: The mismatch matters here only because the bill’s rule would remove these matchups from covered competition.

claims.title: Invasive bodily checks
claims.statement: H.R.28 sets a biological test and no method for checking it. Because of this, schools would come under pressure to use invasive bodily checks. Those checks would expose girls to humiliation, distress or sexual abuse.
claims.classification_reason: Substantive objection repeated in four responses: the text adds no examination procedure, Idaho’s exams came from a separate statute, and most comparable states used birth certificates.
claims.scope_html: This claim is only about bodily checks. It is not about questions based on records, interviews, public accusations, or fear of being challenged. Rejecting this claim blocks only the parts of an argument (routes) that need bodily checks.
claims.background_html: A gynecological exam is a medical exam of female sex organs. The Ninth Circuit is a federal appeals court. The Supreme Court’s June 30, 2026 decision reversed that court’s Idaho judgment, which came after the comparison date.
claims.support_html: Representative Hayes says the bill “provides neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources” [1]. The National Women’s Law Center and Women’s Sports Foundation warn of “a variety of invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [2] and say: “These procedures make all women and girls vulnerable to sexual abuse” [2]. A federal appeals court described Idaho’s law as allowing checks “including gynecological exams.” [3] The bill’s test remains “reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [4]

  • Because Being on a team also brings educational chances. The bill itself names “scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.” [1]
  • Because The ban reaches beyond games to “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1] Conditional upon participation means open only to people on the team.
  • Because The same birth-based rule also restricts nonbinary students it classifies as male. Nonbinary students do not identify only as girls or boys. The Congressional Equality Caucus, a group of members of Congress, explains: “It would also limit the ability of non-binary and intersex students to participate in these programs as well.” [20]
  • Because Girls born with variations in sex traits, called intersex variations, also face uncertain eligibility. The National Women’s Law Center and Women’s Sports Foundation warn: “There is no principled way to apply the bill's unclear language to the many girls and young women born with intersex variations” [2]. They describe the result: “Similar bans have been widely used to push girls and women born with these variations out of sports opportunities and have chilled their participation in school sports.” [2]
  • So Blocking team competition and the activities tied to it takes away chances to learn and advance. [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunities includes transgender, nonbinary and intersex students, which gives a reason to oppose these barriers.
  • Note Permission for “males to train or practice” [1] gives back neither eligibility to compete nor equal access to team places and benefits. Even practice is conditional: it is allowed only “so long as no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport” [1], among other protected opportunities.

In the Clark case, a court upheld keeping boys off a girls’ volleyball team because “due to average physiological differences, males would displace females to a substantial extent if they were allowed to compete for positions on the volleyball team.” [21] The reason was a real difference affecting fair competition, not just that separate teams exist.
  • Because Having been eligible under a testosterone limit does not show equal competitive conditions. Reviewing physical traits after male puberty, researchers Hilton and Lundberg reported that “the muscular advantage enjoyed by transgender women is only minimally reduced when testosterone is suppressed.” [22]
  • So Equal opportunity requires a fair basis for eligibility, not keeping every existing route to scholarships, learning or admission. For these students, the argument must show why this boundary unfairly blocks comparable students. Naming benefits and affected identities does not supply that step.
  • Note This response depends on the disputed claim that an advantage remains. A 2026 review reports: “Current evidence is mostly low certainty and has heterogenous quality but does not support theories of inherent athletic advantages for transgender women over cisgender.” [8]
  • So This response does not reach students who have not gone through male puberty, sports where no advantage has been shown, or eligible girls deterred by uncertainty about intersex variations.

arguments.title: Enforcing the birth-sex rule puts children’s privacy, dignity and bodily safety at risk.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 5 Enforcing the birth-sex rule puts children’s privacy, dignity and bodily safety at risk.

  • Because Schools must apply the rule without a set way to check it. Representative Hayes says: “H.R. 28 provides neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources to ensure that students participating in athletics meet these new standards.” [28]
  • Because A comparable ban in Florida led to questions about a child’s private history. The Associated Press (AP) reported: “They interviewed officials at Monarch and at the daughter's middle and elementary schools, seeking to find out who knew the girl was transgender and when and how her records were changed.” [29]
  • Because The investigation also asked teammates about her body: “When investigators interviewed the Monarch volleyball players, they said the team did not change clothes or shower together, so they were never disrobed with Norton's daughter.” [29] Disrobed means undressed.
  • Because After the investigation began, the girl left the school. AP reported: “That all ended when the investigation began and the girl left Monarch.” [29] It added: “The girl now attends school online.” [29]
  • Because Women’s rights organizations warn that checking sex may involve “forcing women and girls to submit to a variety of invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [2]. They name a further danger: “These procedures make all women and girls vulnerable to sexual abuse” [2].
  • So A nationwide duty to enforce birth-sex eligibility creates grounds for the same kind of intrusive questions, with risks of exposure, humiliation and disrupted schooling and, as those organizations warn, abuse. Protecting children from these harms gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the rule.
  • Note A supporter replies: “There is no requirement for inspections” [2]. That does not answer the risk. The documented records checks and interviews already invaded privacy, and they did not need an exam requirement.
arguments.con_html:
Response The evidence does not establish that the bill would lead to bodily examinations or to sexual abuse resulting from them.

  • Because H.R.28 restricts participation in programs “designated for women or girls.” [1] Its text adds no requirement for bodily examinations.
  • Because AP describes questions about records and knowledge: investigators sought “to find out who knew the girl was transgender and when and how her records were changed.” [29] That account reports no bodily examination.
  • Because Florida’s birth-sex law gives a way to decide eligibility from records: a birth certificate is accepted if its sex statement “was filed at or near the time of the student's birth.” [30]
  • So The step to bodily examinations and sexual abuse rests on an organization’s warning, not on a documented case in this evidence. This response does not answer the documented privacy harms from records checks and interviews, or the disrupted schooling that followed.

Evidence note: The Florida inquiry also examined staff handling of records, and the student's mother faced discipline. NCAA policy already required annual eligibility documentation from transgender women athletes. arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill replaces acceptance of transgender teammates with exclusion required by law.

  • Because On January 14, 2025, Title IX, the federal law against sex discrimination in education, protected participation in at least some cases. In a 2024 case, “The Fourth Circuit ruled that application of the West Virginia law to the plaintiff violated Title IX, because it treated her worse than those similarly situated based on her sex and caused her harm.” [8] The Fourth Circuit is a federal appeals court. Similarly situated means in a comparable position.
  • Because Differences between individuals mattered to that ruling. The court criticized a ban that applied “regardless of whether a particular student has any genuine athletic advantages” [8]. H.R.28 would instead make birth biology and genetics decide the question for every student it classifies as male.
  • Because [NAME] values accepting people even when they disagree. That gives weight to including a classmate despite disagreement about that classmate’s gender, and to hearing the student’s situation before ruling the student out.
  • So The bill would close a path to acceptance that the law then in force protected. Hearing individual students, or choosing inclusion as a school community, could no longer change eligibility under its birth-based rule.
  • Because The restriction also reaches activities tied to team membership. The bill includes “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1]
  • Because Shared sports offer chances to know people. Researchers describe “regular social interaction; opportunities to build positive relationships with teammates and coaches” [9].
  • Because Exclusion also marks students as outsiders. arguments.con_html:

  • Because Accepting people across disagreements leaves room to disagree about rules. [NAME] can listen to a student, understand the student’s situation and accept the student while reaching a different view about team eligibility. The research defining this value says it concerns “accepting and understanding those with life-styles and beliefs different from one’s own.” [11]
  • Because The bill sets a rule for sports eligibility: “For the purposes of this subsection, sex shall be recognized based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1] A decision under that rule does not show how classmates regard or listen to the student.

arguments.title: The bill protects girls’ chances to gain physical and mental health benefits from sports.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill protects girls’ chances to gain physical and mental health benefits from sports.

  • Because Limited team places can mean lost participation.   • Because The bill keeps female competition for those female at birth. It also makes male practice depend on protecting each female’s “opportunity to participate in a practice or competition” [1].
  • So The bill prevents that source of exclusion from female competition and practice. Where a girl has no other team place, this keeps her chance to exercise on a team open.
  • Because The federal health department explains that sports “participation is one way for youth to get the physical activity they need to be fit and healthy.” [15]
  • Because A U.S. study compared girls with boys during Title IX’s expansion of girls’ sports. It reported that the expansion “resulted in greater physical activity and improved weight and body mass.” [16]

arguments.con_html:

  • Because Starling “was bumped down to the JV team.” [14] JV means junior varsity.

  • Because The health study concerns more girls joining sports: “Title IX caused a significant increase in girls’ sports participation.” [16]
  • So That research is about girls added to sports, while the example is about a girl who stayed active. The evidence given does not support the step from being moved down to exercising less. This response does not address a girl cut from a team with limited places and no other place to play.

arguments.title: Enforcing the birth-sex rule opens girls to intrusive checks, sexual abuse and trauma.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 Enforcing the birth-sex rule opens girls to intrusive checks, sexual abuse and trauma.

  • Because The bill sets a birth-sex rule but does not say how to check it. Representative Hayes noted that it provides “neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources” [18].
  • Because Idaho passed an intrusive rule for checking sex. The Ninth Circuit, a federal appeals court, described it as allowing “intrusive medical procedures to verify her sex, including gynecological exams” [19]. A gynecological exam is a medical exam of female sex organs.
  • Because The National Women’s Law Center and Women’s Sports Foundation warn that H.R.28 invites “invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [9] that “make all women and girls vulnerable to sexual abuse” [9].
  • Because Such checks also threaten mental health. The court explained: “The psychological burden of these searches falls not only on transgender women like Lindsay but also on all women and girls who play female athletics.” [19]
  • Because Fear of checks also threatens participation. Representative Randall warned that intrusive questions and examinations would be “dissuading girls' participation in sports” [9]. Dissuading means persuading people not to do something.
  • So The new federal eligibility rule creates risks of bodily intrusion, abuse and distress in an ordinary school activity. By discouraging girls from playing, it also threatens the health benefits of exercise. Avoiding these dangers serves [NAME]’s aim to stay safe and healthy.
arguments.con_html:
Response Idaho’s separate medical-testing rule does not establish that H.R.28 would expose girls to intrusive exams.

  • Because H.R.28 defines sex by “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth” [1] without ordering medical inspections. The House member managing the bill described the intended method: “There is no requirement for inspections, and there is no necessary effort other than going to a person's birth certificate.” [9]
  • Because The Idaho court tied intrusive checks to that state’s separate “sex dispute verification provision” [19]. It also reported: “Most states that have instituted categorical bans on transgender participation in student athletics have verified sex via a student’s birth certificate.” [19]
  • So The argument’s own court source gives a working alternative to intrusive exams under comparable restrictions. Idaho shows that a legislature can choose exams, but it does not show that schools under H.R.28 would choose them over records. The claims of exam-related abuse and trauma depend on that step. This response does not address questions based on records, or fear and withdrawal caused by the possibility of challenges.

The same court reported that most states with categorical bans verified sex through a birth certificate. H.R.28 specifies no verification process. Sources: [19], [1].

Evidence note: On June 30, 2026, after the January 14, 2025 comparison date, the Supreme Court reversed the Fourth Circuit's B.P.J. judgment and the Ninth Circuit's Hecox judgment and sent both back to the lower courts (remanded them). The Fourth Circuit ruling was in force on the comparison date. The decision permits such rules. It does not impose a nationwide requirement like H.R.28, and it calls participation "a debated policy question". It describes the underlying science of retained advantage as subject to ongoing debate. A word search of the full opinion text found no discussion of sex-verification procedures or examinations. Sources: [20].

arguments.title: The bill takes a decision about children’s upbringing away from families and local groups already responsible for it.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill takes a decision about children’s upbringing away from families and local groups already responsible for it.

  • Because The Southern Baptist Convention, a large Christian denomination, teaches that “parents are the primary stewards of and decision-makers for their children, rather than teachers, doctors, or the state” [18]. A steward is someone responsible for caring for something.
  • Because Catholic teaching protects work that smaller groups can do themselves. It calls it an injustice to “assign to a greater and higher association what lesser and subordinate organizations can do.” [19]
  • Because Sports rules are already partly a local responsibility: “Currently, schools, parents, and communities manage youth sports leagues and write rules about who can participate in different sports at different levels.” [14]
  • Because Existing reviews of individual students already consider safety and fairness. The Congressional Research Service describes Illinois’s 2024–25 rules as “requiring approval to participate based on consideration of individual circumstances” [6] and as considering whether “allowing eligibility would be inconsistent with concepts of fairness in competition or present a risk of injury to the participants” [6].
  • Because H.R.28 would remove that choice at covered schools. As Representative Norcross explained: “It inflicts blanket bans without the ability of states, local governments, schools, and parents to make reasonable exceptions.” [20]
  • So Even when parents and a willing school approve a child’s participation after an individual review, the federal rule would bar girls’ competition if it classifies that child as male. Keeping the family and local roles taught by [NAME]’s tradition gives a reason to oppose that loss of authority.
arguments.con_html:
Response The argument has not shown that the particular sports exception being removed belongs to the family and local duties its religious sources protect.

  • Because The cited Baptist resolution places parents’ decisions “under the authority of God, recognizing that they will be held responsible for their choices” [18].
  • Because The Ethics & Religious Liberty Commission, a Southern Baptist agency, explains: “The duty of parental authority is not the right to teach children whatever they desire. Rather, it is normed by what is good, true, and righteous.” [21] Normed by means limited by that standard.
  • Because That same body addressed this sports decision on January 13, 2025: “Schools that allow biological males to participate in female sports programs are discriminating against biological females.” [22]
  • So In this account, approval by parents and a school does not turn that eligibility exception into an act of Christian care or rightful parental teaching. The argument cannot conclude that religious authority protects the exception just because parents and a school want it.
  • Because The Catholic principle of leaving work to smaller groups also serves duties beyond those groups. The same source says: “To ensure the common good, the government of each country has the specific duty to harmonize the different sectoral interests with the requirements of justice” [19]. Harmonize means bring together.
  • Because Illinois’s 2024–25 policy made eligibility a decision for the statewide sports association: “IHSA will make final rulings on student participation.” [23] The association's review considered whether eligibility would be “inconsistent with concepts of fairness in competition or present a risk of injury to the participants” [6].
  • So Showing that a lower body can run a review does not show that its eligibility standard meets the religious account of justice. The argument has not shown that allowing this exception is a duty the cited traditions reserve to families or local groups. Its claim of lost religious authority therefore lacks the needed link.

arguments.title: Disputes over sex eligibility can conflict with religious practices of modesty and intimate privacy.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 Disputes over sex eligibility can conflict with religious practices of modesty and intimate privacy.

  • Because Schools would have to apply the bill’s definition of sex, but it gives no way to check disputed eligibility. Representative Hayes says: “H.R. 28 provides neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources to ensure that students participating in athletics meet these new standards.” [24]
  • Because Women’s sports organizations warn that resulting checks “may include forcing women and girls to submit to a variety of invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [14].
  • Because Questions about intimate matters have occurred under a comparable state ban. The National Women’s Law Center reports that a Florida investigation included “interviews with her teammates on if they saw her undressed.” [25]
  • Because Catholic teaching connects children’s privacy to moral upbringing: “Respect for privacy must be considered in close connection with decency and modesty” [26]. Modesty is keeping the body and private matters covered or private.
  • So Applying the rule in schools that now allow participation would require them to settle disputes about sex eligibility. The Florida account documents intimate questions, and the organizations also warn of invasive checks. For [NAME], keeping the particular religious practices of modesty and intimate privacy supplies the Tradition connection. General safety and dignity are separate reasons.
arguments.con_html:
Response The House member managing the bill identifies a way to use records, which limits the argument about bodily examinations.

  • Because The bill adds a violation of Title IX, the federal education law, for “a recipient of Federal financial assistance” [1] and defines sex by “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth” [1]. Its text sets no examination procedure. A recipient is a school or college that receives federal money.
  • Because The bill’s manager described a way to apply the bill through records: “There is no requirement for inspections, and there is no necessary effort other than going to a person's birth certificate.” [14]
  • Because The Florida source reports a state investigation that included “interviews with her teammates on if they saw her undressed.” [25] That describes questions, not a bodily examination.
  • So The manager’s account of using records relates to the proposed step from this rule to bodily examinations. It does not answer the documented risk of intimate questions, or show that the religious modesty concern disappears. This is a limited response to the examination part only.

  • Because Teammates can help start larger efforts. University of Wisconsin rower Grace Latz said: “I started all of this because my teammates were taking similar classes to me and shared the same values, so it made it easier.” [5]
  • Because The recycling group Latz helped start, called REthink, later reached other parts of the university: “Since then, REthink has expanded beyond the UW athletic department to work with the UW campus, the hospital, the Wisconsin unions, dining services and UW housing.” [5]

  • Because College sailing gives a real example. Harvard University describes one sailor’s wish to protect the environment: “It's that time in the water with her teammates that has driven Hogan-Lopez to learn more about the environment and how to protect it.” [14]

  • Note The exception that lets students “train or practice” [1] does not give back access to competition.

HR28_UNC_support_01.support:
Point 1 The bill protects women’s fair chance to earn sports wins and recognition.

  • Because Male puberty builds strength. Testosterone is a hormone, and a review of research explains that “increases in testosterone due to puberty promote muscular strength” [5].
  • Because The review looked at 24 studies of transgender women who were not athletes. Here, transgender women are people classified male at birth who identify as women. After 12 to 36 months of hormone treatment, the review said: “transwomen likely retain a strength advantage over cisgender women.” [5] Cisgender women are women whose gender identity matches their sex at birth.
  • Because Strength matters in speed and power events: “In sports demanding speed and power, muscular strength and the ability to generate high rates of force are recognised as key determinant in athletic success.” [5]
  • So In events that depend on strength, the bill would keep strength advantages retained from male puberty out of the female category. Giving women a real chance to earn sports rewards serves [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunity and just treatment.

NCAA eligibility on the comparison date used sport-specific testosterone thresholds. CRS reports that some states and school districts allowed participation with no particular requirements or restrictions. CRS is the Congressional Research Service, which does research for Congress. NCAA is the main college sports organization. Sources: [4], [7].
HR28_UNC_support_01.response:
Response The evidence does not settle whether transgender women who train and compete keep the speed and power advantage this fairness argument needs.

  • Because The review says the effects on people who train are not known. GAHT means hormone treatment that matches gender identity: “the effects of GAHT on these parameters, or indeed athletic performance in transgender people who engage in training and competition, remain unknown.” [5]
  • Because The review does not say whether the compared groups trained the same amount: “The levels of physical activity of the transwomen compared with cisgender women in the studies were not reported.” [5]
  • Because A 2024 study measured athletes at one point in time and found mixed results. Compared with cisgender women athletes, transgender women athletes had “higher absolute handgrip strength” [6] but “lower relative jump height” [6]. Relative jump height takes body weight into account.
  • So Strength kept by people who are not athletes does not show an advantage among trained athletes in a speed or power event. The one athlete study points in both directions. Its authors write: “Sports-specific studies are necessary to inform policy-making.” [6] This response does not show that no advantage exists. It also does not address places without hormone limits.

A 2026 British Journal of Sports Medicine systematic review (52 studies) reports pooled comparisons of transgender women and cisgender women as similar on relative lean mass, upper-body and lower-body strength and maximal oxygen consumption. The statistical ranges for those comparisons include zero (no difference), and certainty is rated low or very low. Its conclusion states higher lean mass with comparable fitness and calls the evidence mostly low certainty. A later correction removed three studies, added one and said the main conclusions were unchanged. These are averages for body composition and fitness. The text in this project's evidence collection reports no result by sport for absolute mass, speed, collisions or injuries. Sources: [8], [9].

The review came after the comparison date but before the evidence cutoff. Sources: [8], [9].

A 2026 review says: “Current evidence is mostly low certainty and has heterogenous quality but does not support theories of inherent athletic advantages for transgender women over cisgender.” [4] These sources do not rule out an advantage in a particular sport.

HR28_UNC_support_02.support:
Point 2 The bill protects girls’ places in sports and their chances to gain education, health and leadership benefits.

  • Because Former college swimmer Paula Scanlan told a House committee that places were actually lost: “I know women who have lost roster spots and spots on the podium.” [10] A roster spot is a place on a team. A podium spot is a top finish in a race.
  • Because The bill allows male training or practice only “so long as no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition, scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.” [1]
  • So Where places or sports money are limited, the competition ban and the practice condition protect female athletes from losing them to male participants. For a girl who needs sports money to attend college, protecting that money keeps open a way into education.
  • Because Girls in positive sports programs report better mental health. A 2024 study found: “Girls who play sport in positive environments report significantly lower levels of anxiety and depression than those who previously played or never played.” [11]
  • Because A 2024 survey of U.S. adults who had played girls’ or women’s sports found reported gains in leadership skills: “Half of women (48.6%) credit the skills acquired through sports for their leadership development.” [12]
  • So Keeping a girl’s place in a good program keeps her chance to gain these benefits. Protecting these ways into education, well-being and adult leadership serves [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunities in life.
HR28_UNC_support_02.response:
Response Protecting a place does not by itself show that opportunity has become more equal. This reason depends on the fairness claim in Point 1.

  • Because The bill’s practice exception requires that “no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition, scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.” [1]
  • So Where a place is limited, the bill decides which student holds it. That shows who keeps the benefit. It does not show that this division of places is fairer.
  • Because The mental-health finding is about access to a good program: “Girls who play sport in positive environments report significantly lower levels of anxiety and depression than those who previously played or never played.” [11]
  • Because The leadership finding is about benefits people connect to playing: “Half of women (48.6%) credit the skills acquired through sports for their leadership development.” [12]
  • So These benefits go to whoever holds the place. They do not answer who has a fair claim to it. This reason adds to [NAME]’s equal-opportunity concern only as far as the fairness claim in Point 1 holds. This response does not dispute that some female athletes would keep places and their benefits under the bill.

HR28_UNC_support_03.support:
Point 3 The bill protects physically vulnerable athletes from dangerous matchups and from games lost over safety concerns.

  • Because World Rugby, the international body for the contact sport of rugby, links risk in that sport to “the size, force- and power-producing advantages conferred by testosterone during puberty and adolescence, and the resultant player welfare risks this creates” [13].
  • Because World Rugby's review explains the danger to a smaller player: “Forces and inertia faced by a smaller and slower player during frequent collisions are significantly greater when in contact with a much larger, faster player.” [13]
  • Because World Rugby’s review of 12 months of lowering testosterone, a hormone, concludes that “this comparatively small effect of testosterone reduction allows substantial and meaningful differences to remain.” [13]
  • So In school contact competition such as rugby, excluding male competitors who have gone through male puberty removes this source of size and force mismatch. That protects athletes who are less able to withstand those forces.
  • Because Safety concerns have also cost whole teams games. After Payton McNabb was injured playing volleyball in 2022, her school board voted “to forfeit the remaining varsity and junior varsity volleyball games against Highlands School” [14], which the report describes as “attended by the transgender player.” [14] To forfeit means to give up a game. The report says: “The board cited safety concerns for players.” [14] That player’s status is not confirmed: “It is not possible to verify this athlete was trans.” [15]
